newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish cabinet divided over budget spending.
newsitem.headline: Polish cabinet divided over budget spending.

text.p: Poland's government, divided over how much to curb the budget deficit to stifle domestic demand and how to keep the trade gap under control, resumed on Thursday the debate on the outline of the 1998 national budget.
The government press office said it was not clear if the cabinet would approve the outline, consisting of macroeconomic assumptions, spending and revenue levels, on Thursday.
"The prime minister has limited time on Thursday, so it is not clear if the debate on the budget assumptions will be finished," a press officer said.

The cabinet session, due to decide on the finance ministry proposal to cut the budget gap to 1.9 percent of gross domestic product next year from 2.8 percent planned for 1997, began amid conflicting calls to raise spending and curb the gap even more.

The Polish Peasant Party (PSL), the smaller group in the ruling leftist coalition, has obliged its cabinet members to vote against the finance ministry's proposal, saying it would hit farmers' income, curb investment and boost unemployment.
"This policy will not stimulate exports' growth and will contribute to an increase in unemployment," PSL leader Waldemar Pawlak said on Wedensday.

The ex-communists, the stronger party in the government which has so far supported the finance ministry's policies, dismissed the Peasants' objections as electioneering before the September 21 parliamentary polls.
The ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) can outvote the Peasants during cabinet meetings.
Finance Minister Marek Belka says the budget deficit must be slashed to prevent the trade and current account gap from getting out of control.

Some analysts warn that if the current account deficit, which is forecast to grow to $6 billion this year from $1.35 billion in 1996, expands too much in 1998 Poland might eventually have to devalue the zloty. They say this would boost inflation and undermine economic growth.

But the central bank says the finance ministry proposals do not go far enough and suggests that the 1998 budget should be balanced to help Poland avoid in the future economic hurdles recently experienced by the Czech Republic.
The Czech Republic had to devalue its currency and take strict anti-import measures, after its foreign trade deficit grew too much and industrial output shrank.
The Polish central bank's president Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz said in a newspaper on Thursday that the likelihood of an interest rate rise would grow if next year's deficit was approved at 1.9 percent.
